units.title: Solutions and Their Properties
units.intro: Solution = solute + solvent, homogeneous. Dilute vs concentrated is amount, not “how dangerous”. Saturated: no more solute dissolves at that T. Solubility usually rises with T for solids; gases dissolve better when cold and under pressure.

cards.title: Formula
body: concentration = amount of solute / volume of solution
School: mol/dm³ or g/dm³. Same units top and bottom.

cards.title: Making and talking about a solution
body: Always say the temperature when you quote solubility — “35 g per 100 g water at 20 °C” is a complete sentence; “35 g” is not. A solubility curve slopes up for most solids; a point above the curve is supersaturated, on the curve saturated, below unsaturated.

Concentration arithmetic: convert cm³ to dm³ (÷1000) before you divide. Diluting: moles of solute stay put, only volume grows, so c₁V₁ = c₂V₂. Stirring and powdering speed dissolving; they do not raise the saturated amount — only temperature (for most solids) does that.
Electrolytes: ionic or strong-acid solutions. Non-electrolytes: sugar, ethanol. Weak electrolytes: weak acids that only partly split. That vocabulary prepares Unit 4.

cards.title: 3.1.1 Describing Solutions
body: A solution is composed of a solute and a solvent.
**A solvent** is the substance that dissolves the solute.
The material dissolved is called a **solute**.
Solids, liquids and gases can dissolve in a solvent.

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: Which of the following physical mixtures is classified as a homogeneous mixture (solution)?

steps.text: **Step 1: Define homogeneous mixtures**
Homogeneous mixtures (solutions) have completely uniform composition throughout in a single physical phase.
**Step 2: Classify options**
Sand/water, oil/water, and chalk/water form distinct phases and are heterogeneous.
Salt dissolves completely and uniformly in water, forming a single phase.

cards.answer: A mixture of table salt and water

cards.title: Worked from review
cards.problem: What happens when a single seed crystal of solute is added to a saturated solution of the identical solute at a constant temperature?

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the definition of a saturated solution**
A saturated solution already contains the absolute maximum amount of dissolved solute at that temperature.
**Step 2: Analyze adding more solute**
Any additional solute added to a saturated solution cannot dissolve and will simply sink to the bottom as an undissolved solid.
**Step 3: Final Answer**

cards.answer: It remains undissolved at the bottom of the container.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following represents a solid-in-solid solution (alloy)?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Understand solid solutions**
Solid-in-solid solutions are called alloys, formed by mixing melted metals and allowing them to solidify.

**Step 2: Identify the alloy**
Steel is a solid solution of carbon (nonmetal solute) dissolved in iron (metal solvent).

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The correct option is **Steel**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: How does temperature affect the solubility of most gaseous solutes in liquid solvents?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze gas dissolution thermodynamics**
Dissolving gas in a liquid is an exothermic process. According to Le Chatelier's principle, adding heat shifts the equilibrium to favor the un-dissolved gas phase.

**Step 2: Connect to particle kinetic energy**
At higher temperatures, gas molecules have higher kinetic energy, allowing them to break weak intermolecular attractions with solvent molecules and escape as gas.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
Therefore, gas solubility **decreases as temperature increases**.

cards.q: A solution is formed by dissolving a maximum of 35.9 g of sodium chloride in 100 mL of water at $$ 25^\circ\text{C} $$. This solution is
cards.why: A **saturated solution** contains the maximum amount of solute that can be dissolved in a given amount of solvent at a specific temperature. Since 35.9g is the maximum for $$ NaCl $$ at $$ 25^\circ\text{C} $$, the solution is saturated.

**Step 1: Recall the definition of a saturated solution**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: When a crystal of salt is added to a salt solution in a beaker, the crystal increases at the bottom of the container, then the solution must be
cards.why: If adding a 'seed' crystal causes more salt to precipitate and collect at the bottom, the solution was **supersaturated**. It contained more dissolved solute than it could normally hold at that temperature, and the addition of a crystal triggered crystallization of the excess.

cards.title: Exam question, solved
cards.problem: When a crystal of a solid is added to a solution it dissolves. The solution is:  A) Saturated  B) Unsaturated  C) Supersaturated  D) Can’t be determined  E) None

steps.text: **Step 1.** An **unsaturated** solution is one that can still dissolve more solute at a given temperature.
**Step 2.** If the added crystal dissolves, it means the solution had not yet reached its maximum capacity.

cards.title: Properties of Solution
body: Colligative flavour in this grade: adding solute can raise boiling point and lower freezing point (salt on roads). Conductivity of a solution needs ions (electrolytes).

cards.title: Tip
body: Like dissolves like: polar/ionic in water; oil in oil. Warm a solid to dissolve more; warm a fizzy drink and the gas leaves.

cards.title: 3.3.1 Dissolution of Solutes in Liquids
body: Because the intermolecular forces in both the solute and the solvent are similar, it is easy for the intermolecular forces in the solute to be broken, allowing the solute to move into the spaces between the molecules of the solvent.
The effect of the polarity of the molecules is also noticeable when gases dissolve in water.
H2 and O2 are nonpolar, whereas NH3 and HCl are polar.

cards.title: 3.3.2 Effect of Temperature and Pressure on Solubility
body: The effect of pressure on gas solubility is used in the preparation of carbonated beverages.

cards.title: 3.3.3 Colligative Properties of Solutions
body: The properties of solutions can be divided into two main groups: colligative and non-colligative properties.
Non-colligative are those that depend on the identity of the dissolved solute and the solvent.
All physical properties of a solution that depend on the number of solute particles dissolved in the solution are called **colligative properties**.
**Vaporization** is a process in which a liquid is converted to a vapour.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the relationship between the solubility of a gaseous solute in a liquid and the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid (Henry's Law)?

options.A: Solubility is inversely proportional to pressure.
options.B: Solubility is directly proportional to pressure.
options.C: Pressure has no effect on gas solubility.

cards.why:
**Step 1: State Henry's Law**
Henry's Law states that at a constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid.

**Step 2: Final Answer**
Therefore, **Solubility is directly proportional to pressure.**

cards.title: Step-by-step
cards.problem: What is the relationship between the solubility of a gaseous solute in a liquid and the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid (Henry's Law)?

steps.text: **Step 1: State Henry's Law**
Henry's Law states that at a constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid.
**Step 2: Final Answer**
Therefore, **Solubility is directly proportional to pressure.**

cards.answer: Solubility is directly proportional to pressure.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Which of the following physical properties of a solution is classified as a colligative property?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define colligative properties**
Colligative properties depend solely on the concentration of solute particles, not on their identity. These are vapor pressure lowering, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression, and osmotic pressure.

**Step 2: Match with options**
**Freezing point depression** is a colligative property.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The correct option is **Freezing point depression**.

tips.text: A solution can have variable amounts of solute; but there is a limit to the amount that can dissolve in a given volume of solvent.
A solution in which more solute can still be dissolved is called unsaturated.
The amount of solute that can dissolve in a given volume of solvent is temperature dependent.
The solubility of most solids increases with an increase in temperature.
A curve that shows how the solubility of a solute in a given solvent varies over a temperature range is called a solubility curve.
Solutions are described qualitatively as dilute or concentrated.
A litre of solution that contains 5 g salt is concentrated when compared to a solution that contain 1g salt; but it in turn is dilute relative to a litre of solution that contains 15g of salt.
The concentration of a solution can be described either qualitatively or quantitatively.
The qualitative method uses the terms "dilute" "and" concentrated" to describe the quantity of solute in a solution.
A dilute solution is one that has a relatively low concentration of solute whereas a concentrated solution is one that has a relatively high concentration of solute.
Formula: concentration = amount of solute / volume of solution School: mol/dm³ or g/dm³. Same units top and bottom.

questions.answer: Solute is dissolved; solvent does the dissolving (usually the larger part).
why: The solute is the substance that dissolves (e.g. sugar); the solvent is the substance it dissolves in (e.g. water), usually present in the larger amount.
